slides.say: The accompanying figure shows three right triangles. The marked side lengths are in centimeters. What is C D, in centimeters?
Three right triangles, one next to the other, and we need C D, the bottom side. [short pause] We'll go triangle by triangle, and each one gives us a side for the next one.

[short pause] Start with triangle A B C. The right angle is at A, so B C, thirty-nine, is the hypotenuse, and A B, fifteen, is a leg. We could use the theorem, thirty-nine squared minus fifteen squared. But look at the numbers. Fifteen is five times three, and thirty-nine is thirteen times three. That's the triple five, twelve, thirteen, times three. So A C is twelve times three, which is thirty-six.
at: Start with triangle A B C
The right angle is at A
So A C is twelve times three

slides.say: Now triangle A C E. It's also right-angled at A, with legs A C, thirty-six, and A E, forty-eight. After some practice, these numbers jump out. Thirty-six is three times twelve, and forty-eight is four times twelve. That's three, four, five, times twelve. So the hypotenuse C E is five times twelve, which is sixty.

Now triangle C E D. The right angle is at E, and both legs are sixty. Sixty and sixty aren't in a triple. There is a shortcut for this kind of triangle, and we'll learn it soon. For now, the theorem: C D squared is sixty squared plus sixty squared.
at: The right angle is at E

slides.say: Instead of adding it up, I write it as two times sixty squared, because I know the root will be simpler. The root of two times sixty squared is the root of two, times sixty. So C D is sixty root two, and choice number three is our answer.
at: So C D is sixty root two
and choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Without the triples, we'd have to square numbers like thirty-nine and forty-eight. Noticing the triples saved all of that. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
